controls.label: Output format
controls.help: JPG fills transparent areas with white. Choose WebP or PNG to keep transparency.

controls.label: Quality
controls.help: Lower quality means smaller files. 70–80 is usually hard to tell apart from the original. Ignored for PNG.

controls.label: Max width (px)
controls.help: Optional. Wider images are scaled down to this width; images are never enlarged.

faq.q: Are my images uploaded to a server?
faq.a: No. Compression happens entirely in your browser using your device, so your photos never leave your computer and nothing is stored or logged.

faq.q: How much smaller will my images get?
faq.a: It depends on the image. Photos usually shrink the most. Screenshots and graphics saved as PNG shrink best when you switch to WebP or JPG, or reduce the maximum width.

faq.q: Which output format should I choose?
faq.a: JPG is the safest choice and works everywhere. WebP usually gives the smallest files, but some browsers, notably Safari, can't create WebP files here and will fall back to another format. Use PNG when you need transparency without any quality loss.

faq.q: Does compressing remove metadata such as location?
faq.a: Yes. Re-encoding an image removes camera details and GPS location. The exception is when an image can't be made any smaller: then the original file is kept exactly as it is, metadata included.

faq.q: Why is some image marked as already optimized?
faq.a: If compressing would make a file larger than the original in the same format, the tool keeps the original so you never end up with a bigger file.
